item.title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
item.description:
Skim new method — Machine-checked verification in Rocq of block-encoding-based Hamiltonian simulation compilation, producing circuits with certified error bounds that achieve up to 94% gate reduction relative to PennyLane.

Grade 0.546 · 3.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers”

Figure

Compilation pipeline for Hamiltonian simulation comparing the Trotter-based flow (Trotterization to digital or analog targets) and the verified block-encoding flow (expansion, block encoding, and digital circuit generation).

Asks

Can block-encoding-based Hamiltonian simulation algorithms be end-to-end verified with machine-checked error bounds and compiled efficiently compared to existing compilers?

Before

Unverified block-encoding compilation in PennyLane and Trotter-only verified compilation in QBlue

But

Digital quantum backends only for block-encoding algorithms; practical gate-count advantage over Trotter-based approaches is lost for short simulation times and loose error bounds.

Tools

Rocq proof assistant · block encoding · Taylor and Jacobi-Anger expansions · PennyLane

Abstract

Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to textsfQBlue_textttBE by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a 94% gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

item.title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum k-Cut Problem
item.description:
Skim new method — BT-QAOA decomposes Max-k-Cut into at most 2k−3 standard MaxCut QAOA instances, reducing native CZ gate counts from 10855.2 (k=3) and 9748.8 (k=4) under binary encoding to 1866.4 on 24-vertex random graphs while raising the estimated circuit success probability by over 27 orders of magnitude.

Grade 0.431 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Tackling the Qubit Mapping Problem for NISQ-Era Quantum Devices”

Figure

Compiled native CZ gate counts (left) and estimated circuit success probability (right) plotted against vertex count n for Kn and G(n,1/2) graphs under IBM Torino calibrations.

Asks

Can multiway graph partitioning (Max-k-Cut) be solved via QAOA without direct multistate encodings that inflate qubit counts or circuit depths?

Before

Binary encoding required n⌈log2⁡k⌉ qubits and multiqubit Pauli decompositions (6 to 8 CNOTs per edge per layer for k=3,4), yielding an ESP of roughly 10−32 on 24-vertex random graphs at p=2.

But

Evaluated via noiseless statevector simulations on up to 24-vertex graphs and hardware compilation without experimental execution on the processor.

Tools

Binary-tree recursive partitioning · Standard MaxCut QAOA (p=2) · Qiskit transpilation on IBM Torino architecture

Abstract

The maximum k-cut (Max-k-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the k possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with k. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-k-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most 2k-3 subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after k-1 steps form an approximate solution to the Max-k-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.

item.arxave:action: Assess whether the binary-tree Max-k-Cut decomposition can be run end-to-end from the HPC system as an Annex8_2-style application benchmark, and compare its compiled depth/CZ count against direct binary-encoding QAOA on the spin-qubit topology.

Implement the recursive MaxCut splitting as a circuit-generation layer on top of the existing compiler, using device calibration data to prune bad couplers as the paper does with Qiskit, and expose it through the high-level framework/OpenQASM path.
